          "text": "# MCG 3-29-20: A Quiet Beacon in Leo\n\n*This catalog-numbered galaxy is more than a faint oval: its compact, energetic core marks it as a Seyfert 2.*\n\nIn the spring constellation Leo, a small telescope can turn up a distant island of stars with a surprisingly active heart. MCG 3-29-20 is also cataloged as NGC 3607. Its light has traveled across space to reach us, carrying clues to a galaxy whose calm-looking glow conceals a powerful central engine.\n\nThe galaxy sits at right ascension 11h 16m 55s and declination +18\u00b0 03\u2032 (J2000), in Leo. Catalog data list it as roughly 4.1 by 3.6 arcminutes across\u2014several times the apparent width of Jupiter, though its light is spread thinly over that area. Its listed visual magnitude is about 12.8, so it is a telescopic target rather than a naked-eye sight. [SIMBAD\u2019s NGC 3607 record](https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr/simbad/sim-id?Ident=NGC%203607) identifies it as a Seyfert 2 galaxy.\n\nThat classification points to the galaxy\u2019s nucleus. A Seyfert galaxy is a type of active galaxy: gas falling toward a supermassive black hole can heat up and shine intensely before it disappears from view. In a Seyfert 2, astronomers see strong emission from the active nucleus, but the broad-line region close to the black hole is not directly visible. One explanation is that intervening gas and dust obscure our view of that inner zone. The galaxy\u2019s ordinary starlight remains visible, but the nucleus adds a more energetic chapter to its story.\n\nSIMBAD lists a redshift of about 0.00319, corresponding to a recession velocity near 955 kilometres per second in the record. That figure is not a simple cosmic speedometer: at relatively small distances, a galaxy\u2019s motion within its local region can complicate attempts to infer its distance from redshift alone. For observers, the essential point is that MCG 3-29-20 is far beyond the Milky Way, and its light arrives as a soft, extended patch rather than a sharp point.\n\nTo find it, look in Leo during northern spring evenings, when the constellation climbs high in the south. Start with Delta Leonis (Zosma), the star marking the lion\u2019s hindquarters, then sweep about 2\u00bd degrees south and slightly east with a finder or binoculars. A planetarium app or printed chart set to the galaxy\u2019s coordinates can help distinguish it from nearby field stars. Under a dark sky, try a telescope of 6 inches or more; higher magnification is not always better for a diffuse object, so begin at low or moderate power and use averted vision.
